clue.text: Extract from channel by excellent former laureate

indicators.note: extract from means letters are pulled out of channel, its front pair and last letter, leaving the core

parts.note: fine means excellent, as in a fine performance

explanation.surface: A TV channel airs a clip featuring a fine former poet laureate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extract from' removes CH and L from 'channel', leaving its inner run. The laureate is the Children's Laureate, a post Anne Fine held, not the Poet Laureate.
explanation.definitionFit: The children's author held the post of Children's Laureate from 2001 to 2003, so she is a past holder of that title.

clue.text: Enemy social worker has a go on Ulster street

parts.note: an ant is a worker in a social insect colony
taken as written: a go is an attempt
NI is Northern Ireland, often called Ulster

explanation.surface: A hostile social worker takes a turn on a Belfast street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'social worker' is not a council employee but the worker ant of an insect colony.
explanation.definitionFit: An antagonist is an opponent or adversary.

clue.text: Those linked at home know trees spread around river

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the river letter
spread means the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Home workers know how trees spread out along a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'at home' is part of the definition: home workers linked by computer networks.
explanation.definitionFit: Networkers are people who work connected by computer links, often from home.

clue.text: Sewage put the wrong side in estuary

indicators.note: the right side is swapped for the left: the letter for right is replaced by the letter for left

parts.note: a firth is a Scottish estuary

explanation.surface: Sewage pumped out on the wrong side of an estuary.
explanation.walkthrough: R (right) is the wrong side here, so L (left) replaces it.
explanation.definitionFit: Filth is dirt or foul matter, which raw sewage is.

clue.text: Romanesque correspondent responsible for the 15 and the 7

parts.note: Norman architecture is the English form of the Romanesque style
a mailer is someone who sends mail, a correspondent

explanation.surface: A letter-writer in a round-arched building writes about nudity and death.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 and 7 give NAKED and DEAD: his first novel was The Naked and the Dead.
explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist wrote the war novel The Naked and the Dead in 1948.

clue.text: Cover in partly foreign aircraft

indicators.note: the cover goes in, placed inside the letters for the foreign word
partly means only part of the language word is used, its tail dropped

parts.note: German is a foreign language to an English speaker
a lid is a cover, as on a pot

explanation.surface: Some sort of covering on a partly foreign-built plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' cuts German down to its first three letters; the lid sits inside them, so the cover is literally 'in' the foreign word.
explanation.definitionFit: A glider is an engineless aircraft that flies on air currents.

clue.text: Tate's mate accepts one-party conduct

indicators.note: accepts means the partner's name takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: Lyle partners Tate in the sugar firm Tate & Lyle
I is the Roman numeral for one
a fest is a festival or party

explanation.surface: A friend of Tate's agrees to behave in one-party fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: Tate & Lyle is a British sugar company; IFEST goes inside LYLE after its first L.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifestyle is the way a person lives and behaves, their manner of conduct.

clue.text: Useless people in the Black Hills

definitions.meaning: people who contribute nothing and could be cut from a team
a gold-rush town in the Black Hills of South Dakota

explanation.surface: Layabouts out in the hills of Dakota.
explanation.walkthrough: Deadwood, South Dakota, is the frontier town of Wild Bill Hickok and Calamity Jane.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead wood is an idiom for staff who do no useful work, and Deadwood is a Black Hills town.

clue.text: Not often still red?

definitions.meaning: of meat cooked so lightly that it is still red inside

explanation.surface: A steak that seldom comes out pink enough.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means seldom seen, and of steak means only lightly cooked.

clue.text: Protective expression of disapproval at upsetting beer on line

parts.note: tut is the clicking sound people make to show disapproval

indicators.note: upsetting tips the beer over, so its letters are read backwards

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
RY is short for railway, a railway line

explanation.surface: A tut of disapproval at someone knocking over beer on a railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' turns the beer backwards, and 'at' and 'on' only join the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutelary describes a guardian spirit or power that watches over and shields someone.

clue.text: Temporary relationship with a b-blonde?

parts.note: the stammered b-blonde asks for a word for blonde, fair, said with the same stutter on its first letter

explanation.surface: A fling with a girl whose blondness the speaker can barely get out.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter written into 'b-blonde' tells the solver to stammer the synonym too: FAIR becomes F-FAIR, and A goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An affair is a love relationship outside marriage, usually brief.

clue.text: Lord in France near having certain difficulty with nonconformity

parts.note: a peer is a lord, a member of the nobility
pres is French for near
sure means certain

explanation.surface: A lord living close by in France is sure he will struggle to fit in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Peer pressure pushes people to conform, so it makes being a nonconformist hard.

clue.text: Exclamation (from Plumstead) promising to the 7?

definitions.meaning: a cry of surprise, as uttered by Archdeacon Grantly of Plumstead Episcopi in Trollope's Barchester novels
a fine paradise is good news for the 7 (the dead), whose afterlife lies in the skies

explanation.surface: A cry of surprise from a Trollope parsonage, and a hopeful forecast for the departed.
explanation.walkthrough: Plumstead Episcopi is Archdeacon Grantly's parish in Trollope's Barchester novels, where the archdeacon is given to this cry. 7 refers to DEAD, the first half of 7/22.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a standard cry of surprise, and read literally names a pleasant afterlife in the skies awaiting the departed.

clue.text: Be told rumours of domestic setting in grammar school

parts.note: the hearth is the fireside, the heart of a home

explanation.surface: Pupils pick up gossip about home life at a grammar school.
explanation.definitionFit: To hear things is to pick up gossip or reports, or to imagine sounds.

clue.text: I leave Saddam's henchman as indexed relating to elixirs

indicators.note: leave means the letter I departs from the name

parts.note: Chemical Ali, Saddam Hussein's cousin, listed surname first in an index

explanation.surface: An Iraqi henchman's index entry, missing a letter, turns up with magic potions.
explanation.walkthrough: An index would list 'Chemical Ali' as Ali, Chemical; drop its first I.
explanation.definitionFit: Alchemists sought the elixir of life, so alchemical things relate to such potions.

clue.text: Moved like a serpent losing something of its shape in birthday suit

indicators.note: losing means the letter described next is dropped from the verb

parts.note: snaked means wriggled along like a serpent
a snake's wriggling body is S-shaped, so the letter S is something of its shape

explanation.surface: A snake slithers about, oddly misshapen, wearing nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The serpent's curving shape is the letter S, so 'losing' it removes the S from SNAKED.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in your birthday suit is an idiom for wearing nothing, as at birth.

clue.text: Snags with Spooner to make holes in Yorkshire power station

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words are exchanged

parts.note: to bore is to drill holes in
Drax is a large power station in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Problems drilling into a Yorkshire power station.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of 'bore Drax' gives 'Draw backs' in a non-rhotic British accent.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawbacks are disadvantages or snags.

clue.text: Havoc as played, alternative to 12 to please the 7?

definitions.meaning: chaos, in the idiom 'to play' it, meaning to cause uproar
a jolly underworld as the other choice to a pleasant heaven, offered to the 7, the dead

explanation.surface: Two afterlives on offer to the deceased, one of them pure chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'play merry hell' is a British idiom for causing chaos. 12 is GOOD HEAVENS and 7 is DEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase, as in 'play merry hell', means wild disorder or trouble.

clue.text: High ball concealing uncertain treasure, more like fatty bacon

indicators.note: the high ball hides the other piece inside its letters

parts.note: a skier is a ball hit high into the air, especially in cricket

indicators.note: read as un-certain: the word for certain, sure, is taken away from treasure

explanation.surface: A lofted ball hides a doubtful hoard, oddly compared to streaky rashers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncertain' is read as un-sure: SURE comes out of 'treasure', and the rest goes inside the high ball after its first letter. Streaky bacon is British belly bacon, striped with fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Streaky bacon has layers of fat running through it, so the comparative describes bacon with more fat stripes.

clue.text: Connect for safety in 13

indicators.note: in tells us the letters wanted sit inside the solution to 13, read straight through

parts.note: the cross-reference stands for the 13 down solution, a fireplace phrase

explanation.surface: Wiring advice for a fireplace setting.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside the 13 down solution, beginning at its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To earth an appliance is to wire it to the ground so that stray current runs away harmlessly.

clue.text: Second name of Sikh swallowed by fish in Norfolk garden centre

indicators.note: the fish swallows the rest, taking those letters into its middle

parts.note: bream is a freshwater fish
Singh is the surname taken by Sikh men

explanation.surface: A Sikh's second name gulped down by a fish at a Norfolk garden centre.
explanation.walkthrough: Bressingham, in Norfolk, an English county, is known for its gardens and steam museum.
explanation.definitionFit: Bressingham Gardens is a well-known nursery and garden centre near Diss in Norfolk.

clue.text: Poet of the sweet spring has direction about tree

indicators.note: about means the direction goes around the tree

parts.note: NE is northeast, a compass direction
the ash is a tree

explanation.surface: A spring poet points the way around a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Nashe's song begins 'Spring, the sweet spring'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Nashe, Elizabethan writer, wrote the poem 'Spring, the sweet spring'.

clue.text: See 7
A container with an opening

parts.note: a jar is a container

explanation.surface: A jar with its lid off.
explanation.definitionFit: A door left ajar is slightly open.

clue.text: Article evoking protest

definitions.meaning: an article is a thing or item
to protest is to raise an objection, a verb

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece that stirs up complaints.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the word means an item or thing; as a verb it means to raise an objection.

clue.text: Not breaking barrier for us — nobis in translation, more or less

indicators.note: translation here means converting the words into another form, so their letters are reordered

parts.note: C stands for circa, Latin for about, so more or less

explanation.surface: A Latin lesson: nobis means for us, roughly speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: Nobis is Latin for 'for us', so the surface poses as a translation note; 'in translation' is the anagram signal, and C (circa) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A subsonic aircraft flies below the speed of sound, so it does not break the sound barrier.

clue.text: Make toe the line, suppressing union by force

indicators.note: suppressing holds the union down inside the drill word

parts.note: to dress soldiers is to line them up exactly, toes level

explanation.surface: Bosses impose discipline, crushing the union by brute force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make toe the line' is the military sense of dress, aligning ranks on parade.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress means coercion, pressure or threats used to compel someone.

clue.text: Backing 1 down leaving (for ever) Sale

indicators.note: leaving says the enemy's letters go out of the words that follow, from scattered places

parts.note: no coincidence: the enemy's letters are removed from these words and Sale, and what is left runs straight through
the 1 down solution is an enemy, which is a foe

explanation.surface: A rugby fan stops supporting a rival who is leaving Sale for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 down is ANTAGONIST, an enemy, so FOE; F and O leave the front of 'for ever Sale' and E its end. Sale is a rugby club in Greater Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: A reversal is a going backwards or turning round, the same as backing.
